new_en: [9] Most of it is closed, etc. If one made tzitzit on it and afterward opened most of it, they are invalid, as stated in seif 5. It requires consideration whether the opening through which the hands are inserted, where the garment has no sleeves, also combines with the majority of the garment that is open. At first glance, since Beit Yosef derives this rule of the majority from seif 4 concerning the majority of a garment, and there it appears that even when leather lies between 1 section of cloth and another they combine, this opening too should combine. Likewise, Beit Yosef in siman 362, seif 8, regarding a breached area greater than the standing area, combines the breaches. [10] And one may not go out, etc. Levush explains that this means into a public domain. This implies that a karmelit is permitted because a doubt concerning a rabbinic prohibition is treated leniently, and Olat Tamid writes likewise. Magen Avraham disagrees and writes that one may not intentionally enter into a doubtful rabbinic prohibition. In my view, the Sages did not enact their decree in a case of doubt. Levush writes that no blessing is recited. Magen Avraham writes that if most of the tallis is cloth and the remainder leather it is obligated in tzitzit, and the reverse likewise follows the majority. If the tallis is leather and cloth is sewn beneath it, it is exempt, and conversely it is obligated, because that which is beneath is secondary to the principal garment.

Time-bound. Rambam writes this because he holds that prayer is a Torah-level positive commandment, as it is written, 'and to serve Him with all your heart,' etc. By Torah law, however, once a day is sufficient, in whatever wording one wishes. Therefore the custom developed that most women do not pray regularly, because immediately in the morning, near the time of washing their hands, they recite some request, and by Torah law that is sufficient. It is possible that the Sages likewise did not obligate them beyond this. Ramban holds that prayer is rabbinic, and this is also the view of most authorities. See Pri Chadash, Sefer Megillat Esther, and Sefer Lev Sameach. Semak writes that there is a mitzvah to pray in a time of distress. See Tosafos, Berachos 20b. To educate them. Nevertheless, one may give them food before prayer. Magen Avraham.

1) [Seif 1] If one is uncertain whether he prayed, he returns and prays. Although in other rabbinic matters we rule leniently in a case of doubt, prayer is a plea for mercy, so we act stringently and he may pray again, for it would be desirable that a person pray and seek mercy all day. Levush, seif 3. Although Levush, who gives this reason, holds that prayer is rabbinic, as stated above in siman 106, letter 7, the same rationale applies even according to those who hold that prayer is a Torah obligation. As explained there, even according to that view the number of daily prayers is rabbinic. By Torah law 1 prayer a day is sufficient and the other prayers are rabbinic. Yet here the ruling is stated without distinction: if one is uncertain whether he prayed, he repeats the prayer, whether Shacharit, Minchah, or Maariv. Even if he already prayed another prayer and thereby fulfilled the Torah obligation, if he is uncertain about this prayer he repeats it. Why, when a rabbinic doubt is normally treated leniently? The reason must be that prayer is mercy and therefore we act stringently, as Levush explains. Maamar Mordechai, letter 3, writes likewise and rejects Olat Tamid, letter 2. 2) There, he returns and prays. He should stipulate: if I did not pray, this is my obligatory prayer; if I did pray, this is a voluntary prayer. Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba; Levush; Olat Tamid; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Ateret Zekenim, letter 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 1. Eshel Avraham, letter 2, writes that if he is uncertain whether he prayed and the time has passed, he should make it up with the adjoining prayer and make this stipulation. It appears that according to our practice, under which we do not offer voluntary prayers, as will be explained below in seif 4, he should not do this. It is sufficient that within the proper time one who is uncertain may pray conditionally; after the time has passed we should not add to that leniency. See the next letter and letter 20 below. Moreover, Eshel Avraham himself, in siman 108, letter 2, again expresses doubt and does not resolve the matter. Therefore what we have written is primary. 3) There, he returns and prays. The wording implies an obligation to repeat the prayer. Rashba writes so in Responsa, siman 91, and Lechem Mishneh, chapter 10 of the Laws of Prayer, law 6, understands Rabbeinu Yonah this way. In Chiddushei Rashba, however, he cites a Gaon, as brought by Beit Yosef, whose words imply that it is not an obligation but a permission: if he wishes, he may repeat the prayer. Pri Chadash, letter 1, agrees, as does Maharshal in Chochmat Shlomo on Tosafos, Berachos 21a. Even according to those who hold that one is obligated to repeat, Pri Megadim in Eshel Avraham, letter 1, writes that for Maariv one is not obligated to repeat, because although Maariv was accepted as obligatory, that applies to certainty, not doubt. Likewise, regarding Shabbos and Yom Tov prayers, even Shacharit and Minchah, one does not repeat because of doubt, since one cannot stipulate that if he already prayed the repetition should be voluntary, as voluntary prayer is not offered on Shabbos or Yom Tov. See there, and see below, letter 8, and siman 124, letter 54. 4) There, and he need not introduce anything new. There is no greater innovation than the fact that he is praying because of doubt, and it may be that the entire prayer is obligatory because perhaps he did not pray previously. Beit Yosef; Levush, seif 3; Shulchan Aruch HaRav there. Some authorities nevertheless hold that even when repeating because of doubt, he should introduce some new request. Bach writes so according to Rav Hai Gaon. It is proper to take his words into account, because there is no concern in adding such a request; even in an obligatory prayer one may add a personal request, as stated at the beginning of siman 119. Chesed LaAlafim, letter 1.

[7] And not from remnants of the warp, etc. One should not object that it would in any event be invalid because it had not been spun for the sake of tzitzit. It can be explained that initially he wove the threads for the sake of tzitzit and afterward wove a garment from them. See Rosh, who gives the reason that attachment must be performed for its sake. This implies that if he detached the threads from there and made tzitzit from them, they are valid, provided that they had been spun for the sake of tzitzit. Rabbeinu Yeruham, page 169, writes that the reason is that spinning must be for its sake. This is puzzling; examine carefully, for I have abbreviated. According to Rambam, Shulchan Aruch, and Levush, however, it appears that even if he detached them from there they remain invalid. [8] Because of degradation of the mitzvah, etc. At first glance this would imply that after the fact they are valid, and this is also the apparent wording of Shulchan Aruch and Levush. Taz and Nachalat Tzvi, however, interpret Shulchan Aruch to mean that even after the fact they are forbidden, in accordance with Rambam. I also found that Baal HaMaor gives another reason: the corner must be of the same material as the garment. These materials are unfit for making a garment because they are wool waste. According to this reason, they are certainly invalid even after the fact.

[9] They are valid, etc. This is because the owner acquires them through despair and a physical change. Some say that even after the fact they are invalid, because this is a change that can return to its original state (Levush). Taz agrees with this latter view, but not for Levush's reason. Rather, he prohibits it because it is a mitzvah performed through a transgression. Levush's reason is difficult, for in Choshen Mishpat there, seif 2, it is ruled that a change of name effects acquisition even if the object can return to its original state, and here too there is a change of name. This also resolves the difficulty raised by Olat Tamid, quoting Shiyurei Knesset HaGedolah, against Rama's ruling that if he spun the stolen wool, etc., it is valid: they object that a reversible change does not effect acquisition. There is no difficulty, because here there is also a change of name. Nevertheless, as a matter of law it is all forbidden, as I wrote in the name of Taz. Yet Taz himself is difficult, for below, siman 649, seif 2, it is explained that where there is despair together with a change, the item is not disqualified as a mitzvah performed through a transgression. One can answer that since the change occurs through making the wool into threads, and we rule that spinning must be performed for the sake of the mitzvah, the change itself is accomplished with the assistance of the mitzvah. It is therefore comparable to one who consecrates a stolen animal, as Tosafos write in Bava Kamma 67a. Yet this too is difficult, because Taz challenges Beit Yosef, who interpreted Rambam here as referring to a change that can return to its original state. Taz writes: 'I am astonished that this holy mouth overlooked the Gemara in the first chapter of HaGozel, where it is explained that whitening wool is a change that cannot return to its original state. One who stole wool and made threads from it must already have whitened it, for without prior whitening it cannot be made into threads.' He therefore interprets Rambam on the basis of a mitzvah performed through a transgression. Rashi indeed explains there that he first whitens it and afterward spins it. If so, however, the change took place before the spinning. Moreover, why did Taz object to Beit Yosef? Rambam may be speaking of one who stole white wool and then spun it into threads, just as the Gemara establishes the Mishnah concerning one who stole wool and made a garment from it as referring to stolen wool that had already been spun. In truth, one may ask why the Gemara did not answer that it refers to white wool that he then spun and made into a garment, but this can be resolved. Rambam's words can certainly be explained this way. Taz further challenges Beit Yosef's interpretation that Rambam speaks before the owner's despair. If so, why is a Scriptural verse needed to disqualify it? In Bava Kamma the Gemara asks that before despair no verse is necessary. My father and teacher answered that a verse is required here because there is a physical change. This is somewhat difficult because the Gemara is discussing an offering, where there is also a change of name, and nevertheless asks why a verse is needed. In my humble opinion there was never a difficulty, for the verse can be needed for a case where one stole threads, which remain invalid even after despair. This must indeed be how Nimukei Yosef, who holds that one who stole wool and made threads from it has valid tzitzit, establishes the verse. Another answer follows Tosafos, Sukkah 30a, who write that only regarding consecrated property does the Gemara ask why a verse is needed, since otherwise the item is ordinary property. See below, siman 649, in Eliyahu Zuta, and the introduction to Beit Yaakov.

One who enters. See Taz. It is possible that 'prohibition and permission' refers to matters of forbidden and permitted foods and to monetary law. 'Halachic ruling' applies to Shabbos and similar matters, and in Even HaEzer to gittin and the like. 'Study' applies even when the matter has no practical legal consequence. See the explanation in Beit Yosef, Levush, Eliyah Rabbah, and Taz. Regarding the statement, 'I toil and they toil; I receive reward and they do not receive reward. I run and they run; I run toward life in the World to Come, and they run toward the pit of destruction,' in my humble opinion, based on Rabbeinu Yonah, the repetition of 'I' teaches that when I see days passing I take care to run and prepare provisions for the journey. This is the meaning of 'I run toward the World to Come,' analogous to 'it hastens toward its place, where it rises.' They, however, do not prepare provisions, because they believe there is no reward and punishment and that the grave alone is their permanent home. Why, then, should they perform mitzvot? This is the meaning of 'their inward thought is that their houses will endure forever.' They believe so, but it is not so, for the soul is taken out and judged. See Levush.

1) [Seif 1] We begin to say in the second blessing, 'Mashiv haruach,' etc. The reason is that just as resurrection of the dead gives enduring life, so rain sustains life continually. Tur; Levush; Taz, seif katan 1; Olat Tamid, letter 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 1. 2) There, we begin to say in the second blessing, etc. It does not open with 'Blessed' because it is adjacent to the preceding blessing. Tur. The same applies to all the blessings through the end of the Amidah. Levush; Ateret Zekenim, letter 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav there. See above at the beginning of siman 113. 3) One should pronounce 'Atah Gibor' with a dagesh in the gimel. Mateh Moshe, siman 125, in the name of Tziyoni; Knesset HaGedolah, Hagahot HaTur, letter 1; Olat Tamid there; Ateret Zekenim there; Eliyah Rabbah, letter 1; Shalmei Tzibbur, page 115d; Kaf HaChayyim, siman 15, letter 22. Sefer Einei HaEdah, page 28a, writes that during the blessing Atah Gibor one should have in mind the Divine Name represented by the initials AGLA, as a segulah for success and favor; see there. Ruach Chaim, letter 3; Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Beshalach, letter 13. 4) There, in the Mussaf prayer of the final Yom Tov of Sukkot, etc. Meaning, one begins mentioning rain in Mussaf on the first day of the final Yom Tov of Sukkot and continues through Shacharit on the first day of Pesach, inclusive. Tur; Levush. 5) There, in the Mussaf prayer of the final Yom Tov, etc. We do not begin at Maariv because not everyone is in the synagogue, and the congregation would become divided, with some mentioning rain and others not. We do not begin at Shacharit so that no one will suppose that it had already been mentioned the previous evening and then, in the following year, begin at night. There is another reason: Rabbi Chaggai bar Padas said that an individual may not mention rain until the prayer leader does so. This means that the prayer leader must announce 'Mashiv haruach' aloud before the prayer, which cannot be done at Shacharit because redemption must be joined immediately to the Amidah. So writes the Rosh based on the Yerushalmi, cited by Beit Yosef; Derishah, letter 1; Taz, seif katan 2; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Shulchan Aruch HaRav there. The Yerushalmi gives another reason. Rabbi Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yehudah's reason is that the festivals should depart with dew, because dew is beneficial. Rosh explains that this reason concerns beginning the mention of rain rather than ceasing it, because on Yom Tov everyone comes to synagogue in the evening and the first reason is therefore insufficient. Thus they arrange matters so that dew is still mentioned during the festival at Maariv and Shacharit. Beit Yosef and Derishah cite this. See the next letter and letter 7. 6) In some countries the custom is to mention rain on Hoshana Rabbah. They do not act properly. If, however, they announce 'Mashiv haruach,' etc. on Hoshana Rabbah so that people begin at night on Shemini Atzeret, there is some basis for the custom. Radbaz, volume 1, siman 240; Knesset HaGedolah, Hagahot HaTur; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1. From the words of the Arizal in Shaar HaKavanot, discourse 9 on Sukkot, and Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaLulav, chapter 8, it appears that the proper time for saying 'Mashiv haruach umorid hageshem' begins specifically with Mussaf of Shemini Atzeret and not before, for a kabbalistic reason explained there. See the next letter. 7) On the night of the final Yom Tov of Sukkot, if one mentioned rain in place of dew, Gan HaMelech, siman 146, rules that he does not repeat the Amidah, and Yad Aharon cites him. Erech HaShulchan, letter 1, writes that this is only according to the first reason of the Rosh in the name of the Yerushalmi, that it would have been fitting to mention rain at Maariv were it not for the concern that the congregation would become divided. According to the second reason, however, that the festivals should depart with dew, one who mentioned rain on the night of the final Yom Tov must repeat. Even on the first night of Pesach, when we do not cease at Maariv in order to avoid division, it is possible that one who failed to mention rain must repeat, since the enactment was not to cease until Mussaf. Maariv and Shacharit therefore retain the law of the preceding days, and changing the fixed formula requires repetition. Nevertheless, Shalmei Tzibbur, page 121c, rules like Gan HaMelech that he does not repeat. So rule Chida in Kesher Gudal, siman 14, letter 14; Siddur Beit Oved, laws of dew and rain, letter 6; and Derech HaChaim, letter 3, that if one mistakenly said 'Mashiv haruach,' etc. at Maariv of Shemini Atzeret or at Shacharit, he does not repeat. Mishnah Berurah, letter 2. Likewise, if one erred at Maariv of Pesach, Shacharit, or Mussaf, for Ashkenazim who still mention rain in Mussaf as stated in seif 3 in the Rama, and omitted 'Mashiv haruach,' he does not repeat. Derech HaChaim, letter 8; Mishnah Berurah, letter 3.
